question.explanation:
To find $\lambda,$ we want to match the expression \[ \mathbf{c} = \dfrac{4}{3}\mathbf{a} + \lambda \mathbf{b}. \]

We are given that one of the components is $\dfrac{4}{3}\mathbf{a}.$ So, we first draw the vector $\dfrac{4}{3}\mathbf{a}$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $\dfrac{4}{3}\mathbf{a}.$ Then \[ \mathbf{c} = \overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PC}. \]

In $\bigtriangleup OPC,$ we have:

  • $PC = \dfrac{1}{4}|\mathbf{b}|$

  • $\overrightarrow{PC}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{PC} = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{b}.$

Additionally, \begin{align*} \mathbf{c} &= \overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PC} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{3}\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $\mathbf{c} = \dfrac{4}{3}\mathbf{a} + \lambda \mathbf{b} = \dfrac{4}{3}\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{b}.$

Since $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{b},$ we get: \[ \lambda = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{4}}. \]

question.text: Consider the picture above. Given that $\mathbf{c}=\lambda\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b}$, find $\lambda.$
question.explanation:
To find $\lambda,$ we want to match the expression \[ \mathbf{c} = \lambda \mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}. \]

We are given that one of the components is $3\mathbf{b}.$ So, we first draw the vector $3\mathbf{b}$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $3\mathbf{b}.$ Then \[ \mathbf{c} = \overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PC}. \]

In $\bigtriangleup OPC,$ we have:

  • $PC=|\mathbf{a}|$

  • $\overrightarrow{PC}$ and $\mathbf{a}$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{PC}=\mathbf{a}.$

Additionally, \begin{align*} \mathbf{c} &= \overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PC} \\[5pt] &= 3\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{a}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $\mathbf{c}=\lambda\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b}.$

Since $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{a},$ we get: \[ \lambda=1 \]

question.explanation:
To find $\lambda,$ we want to match the expression \[ \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a} + \lambda \mathbf{b}. \]

We are given that one of the components is $\mathbf{a}.$ So, we begin with the vector $\mathbf{a},$ and then find the remaining vector needed to reach the point $C.$

Note that in $\bigtriangleup OAC,$ we have:

  • $AC = 3|\mathbf{b}|$

  • $\overrightarrow{AC}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overrightarrow{AC} = 3\mathbf{b}.$

Additionally, \begin{align*} \mathbf{c} &= \overrightarrow{OA} + \overrightarrow{AC} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a} + \lambda \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b}.$

Since $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{b},$ we get: \[ \lambda = 3 \]

question.text: Consider the picture above. Given that $\mathbf{c} = \lambda \mathbf{a} + 4\mathbf{b},$ find $\lambda.$
question.explanation:
To find $\lambda,$ we want to match the expression \[ \mathbf{c} = \lambda \mathbf{a} + 4\mathbf{b}. \]

We are given that one of the components is $4\mathbf{b}.$ So, we first draw the vector $4\mathbf{b}$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

Let $P$ be the endpoint of the vector $4\mathbf{b}.$ Then \[ \mathbf{c} = \overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PC}. \]

In $\triangle OPC,$ we have:

  • $PC = 3|\mathbf{a}|$

  • $\overrightarrow{PC}$ and $\mathbf{a}$ have opposite directions

Hence, $\overrightarrow{PC} = -3\mathbf{a}.$

Additionally, \begin{align*} \mathbf{c} &= \overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PC} \\[5pt] &= 4\mathbf{b} - 3\mathbf{a}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $\mathbf{c} = \lambda \mathbf{a} + 4\mathbf{b} = -3\mathbf{a} + 4\mathbf{b}.$

Since $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{a},$ we get: \[ \lambda = -3 \]

exampleAnswers.title: Finding Two Scalar Factors in a Linear Combination

question.text: Consider the picture above. Given that $\mathbf{c}=\lambda\mathbf{a}+\mu\mathbf{b}$, find $\lambda$ and $\mu.$
question.explanation:
In $\bigtriangleup OAC$ shown above, we have:

  • $OA=3|\mathbf{a}|$

  • $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\mathbf{a}$ have opposite directions

Hence, $\overrightarrow{OA}=-3\mathbf{a}.$

Similarly:

  • $AC=2|\mathbf{b}|$

  • $\overrightarrow{AC}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ have opposite directions

Hence, $\overrightarrow{AC}=-2\mathbf{b}.$

Additionally, \begin{align*} \mathbf{c} &= \overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AC} \\[3pt] &= -3\mathbf{a}-2\mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $\mathbf{c}=\lambda\mathbf{a}+\mu\mathbf{b}=-3\mathbf{a}-2\mathbf{b}.$

Since $\mathbf{a} \nparallel \mathbf{b},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

  • $\lambda=-3$ and $\mu=-2$

example.title: Finding Two Scalar Factors in a Linear Combination

question.text: Consider the picture above. Given that $\mathbf{h}=\lambda\mathbf{f}+\mu\mathbf{g}$, find $\lambda$ and $\mu.$
question.explanation:
In $\bigtriangleup OFH$ shown above, we have

  • $OF=\dfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{f}|$
  • $\overrightarrow{OF}$ has the opposite direction to $\mathbf{f}$

Hence, $\overrightarrow{OF}=-\dfrac 1 2\mathbf{f}.$

Similarly:

  • $FH=2|\mathbf{g}|$
  • $\overrightarrow{FH}$ has the opposite direction to $\mathbf{g}$

Hence, $\overrightarrow{FH}=-2\mathbf{g}.$

Additionally,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{h} &= \overrightarrow{OF}+\overrightarrow{FH} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac1 2\mathbf{f}-2\mathbf{g} . \end{align*}

Consequently, $\mathbf{h}=\lambda\mathbf{f}+\mu\mathbf{g}=-\dfrac1 2\mathbf{f}-2\mathbf{g}.$

Since $\mathbf{f} \nparallel \mathbf{g},$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients, we get:

  • $\lambda=-\dfrac 1 2$ and $\mu=-2$

exampleAnswers.title: Expressing a Vector That Satisfies a Ratio in Terms of Known Vectors

question.text: Consider the diagram above, where $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a},$ $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf{b}$, and $T$ divides $\overline{AB}$ in the ratio $AT:TB = 1:1.$ Find $\overrightarrow{OT}.$
question.explanation:
From the diagram, we see that \[ \overrightarrow{OT} = \overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AT}. \]

We're told that $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a},$ so we just need to work out $\overrightarrow{AT}.$

First, from $\triangle OAB,$ we have

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{AB}&=\overrightarrow{AO}+\overrightarrow{OB} \\[3pt] &= -\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB} \\[3pt] &= -\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b} \\[3pt] &= \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}. \end{align*}

Since $AT:TB=1:1,$ we have

\[ \overrightarrow{AT}=\dfrac{1}{2}\overrightarrow{AB}=\dfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}). \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{OT} &= \overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AT} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{a} + \dfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}. \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing a Vector That Satisfies a Ratio in Terms of Known Vectors

question.text: Consider the diagram above, where $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a},$ $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf{b}$ and $C$ divides $\overline{AB}$ in the ratio $AC:CB=5:1.$ Find $\overrightarrow{OC}.$
question.explanation:
From the diagram, we see that \[ \overrightarrow{OC} = \overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AC}. \]

We're told that $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a},$ so we just need to work out $\overrightarrow{AC}.$

First, from $\triangle OAB,$ we have

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{AB}&=\overrightarrow{AO}+\overrightarrow{OB} \\[3pt] &= -\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB} \\[3pt] &= -\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b} \\[3pt] &= \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}. \end{align*}

Since $AC:CB=5:1,$ we have

\[ \overrightarrow{AC}=\dfrac{5}{6} \overrightarrow{AB}=\dfrac{5}{6}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}). \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{OC} &= \overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AC} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{a} + \dfrac{5}{6}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6}\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{5}{6}\mathbf{b}. \end{align*}
